SUCCESSOR LIABILITY WHEN BUYING A BUSINESS'S ASSETS (RAY V. ALAD CORP.; CORP. CODE § 1107; REV. & TAX. CODE §§ 6811–6814; UNEMP. INS. CODE §§ 1731–1732; LAB. CODE § 200.3) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Pat Morgan

SUCCESSOR LIABILITY IN AN ASSET PURCHASE — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's acquisition of assets of the business known as Acme, Inc. from Pat Morgan, recorded here as closing on November 15, 2026. It describes what California courts and statutes say about when a buyer of a business's assets becomes answerable for the seller's pre-existing debts and liabilities: the general rule of non-liability stated by the California Supreme Court in Ray v. Alad Corp. (1977) and its four traditional exceptions (express or implied assumption, de facto merger or consolidation, mere continuation, and fraudulent transfer); the product-line exception Ray created for strict products liability and the Court of Appeal's refusal to extend it; the equitable character of the doctrine; the contrasting rule for a statutory merger under Corporations Code section 1107; and three statutory successor-liability regimes that operate independently of the case law — the Revenue and Taxation Code's sales and use tax withholding and clearance-certificate provisions, the Unemployment Insurance Code's parallel provisions for employer contributions, and Labor Code section 200.3's successorship rule for unpaid wage judgments. Whether Jordan Lee's transaction with Pat Morgan falls within any of these rules, what liabilities Acme, Inc. carried at closing, what the purchase agreement says about assumption of liabilities, and what consideration was paid are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and a closing date here does not itself establish that any rule described below applies to the transaction, and this sheet states what the courts and statutes say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular acquisition, claim, or defense.

THE GENERAL RULE: A BUYER OF CORPORATE ASSETS DOES NOT TAKE ON THE SELLER'S LIABILITIES, SUBJECT TO FOUR TRADITIONAL EXCEPTIONS
The California Supreme Court's decision in Ray v. Alad Corp. (1977) opens its legal discussion with the rule ordinarily applied when one corporation purchases the principal assets of another. As the court formulated it, the purchaser does not assume the seller's liabilities unless one of four things is true: (1) there is an express or implied agreement of assumption; (2) the transaction amounts to a consolidation or merger of the two corporations; (3) the purchasing corporation is a mere continuation of the seller; or (4) the transfer of assets to the purchaser is for the fraudulent purpose of escaping liability for the seller's debts. The court described the resulting insulation of an asset purchaser from its predecessor's liabilities as having the undoubted advantage of promoting the free availability and transferability of capital. The Court of Appeal restated the same four-part formulation in Franklin v. USX Corp. (2001), quoting an earlier decision: where one corporation sells or transfers all of its assets to another, the latter is not liable for the debts and liabilities of the former unless the purchaser expressly or impliedly agrees to the assumption, the transaction amounts to a consolidation or merger, the purchaser is merely a continuation of the seller, or the transaction is entered into fraudulently to escape liability for debts. Each of the four exceptions, and the separate product-line exception Ray went on to create for strict products liability, is taken up in the clauses that follow.

THE FIRST EXCEPTION: EXPRESS OR IMPLIED AGREEMENT TO ASSUME THE SELLER'S LIABILITIES, AND WHAT THE PURCHASE AGREEMENT'S WORDS DECIDE
The first exception turns on the acquisition agreement itself. In Ray v. Alad Corp., the Supreme Court examined the sale agreement and found that the only provisions for any assumption of the seller's liabilities were that the buyer would accept and pay for materials the seller had previously ordered in the regular course of its business and would fill the seller's uncompleted orders, holding the seller harmless from any liability for failure to do so; the possibility of liability for defects in products the seller had already made was not specifically discussed and no provision was made for it. On those facts the court held there was no express or implied agreement to assume liability for injury from the seller's previously manufactured products. Franklin v. USX Corp. (2001) shows the same analysis producing the same result decades later: the bill of sale there contained specific and clear provisions on the buyer's general nonassumption of liability, stating that the transfer was made without the assumption by the buyers of any of the seller's liabilities except those specifically enumerated, and the enumerated assumptions covered only business obligations such as contracts, purchase orders, unfilled sales orders, performance bonds, and indemnity contracts. Because that purchase agreement was unambiguous and fully integrated, the Court of Appeal held that the trial court erred in considering extrinsic evidence to vary or alter its terms, and that no assumption of the tort liabilities at issue had occurred.

THE SECOND AND THIRD EXCEPTIONS: DE FACTO MERGER AND MERE CONTINUATION, AND THE ROLE OF INADEQUATE CONSIDERATION
Ray v. Alad Corp. describes the second exception — a transaction that amounts to a consolidation or merger — as one invoked where one corporation takes all of another's assets without providing any consideration that could be made available to meet the claims of the other's creditors, or where the consideration consists wholly of the purchaser's stock, promptly distributed to the seller's shareholders in conjunction with the seller's liquidation. For the third exception, Ray states that California decisions finding an asset purchaser to be the seller's mere continuation have imposed liability only on a showing of one or both of two factual elements: no adequate consideration was given for the predecessor's assets and made available for meeting the claims of its unsecured creditors, or one or more persons were officers, directors, or stockholders of both corporations. Because the buyer in Ray paid more than $207,000 in cash and there was no overlap of officers, directors, or shareholders, neither exception applied there. The Court of Appeal in Franklin v. USX Corp. (2001) treated the two exceptions as sharing one crucial factor — whether adequate cash consideration was paid for the predecessor's assets — and held that the common denominator that must be present to avoid the general rule of non-liability is the payment of inadequate consideration, noting that no California case it had found had imposed successor liability for personal injuries on a corporation that paid adequate cash consideration. A later Court of Appeal panel in Cleveland v. Johnson (2012) read the cases differently: it observed that the Supreme Court has not decided whether inadequate consideration is essential, that Ray's "one or both" phrasing suggests it is not, that no single factual element standing alone would probably establish or negate successor liability, and it declined to require a plaintiff to prove inadequacy of the consideration. Cleveland also repeated the Supreme Court's statement in Beatrice Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1993) that even when the same persons are officers or directors of both corporations, liability is not imposed on the acquiring corporation when recourse to the debtor corporation is available and the two corporations have separate identities.

AN EQUITABLE DOCTRINE, EXAMINED ON ITS OWN FACTS, AND NOT CONFINED TO CORPORATION-TO-CORPORATION TRANSFERS
Although successor liability is almost always couched in terms of liability flowing from one corporation to another, the Court of Appeal in Cleveland v. Johnson (2012) held that the principles underlying the mere-continuation theory are not confined to corporations: a corporation may be a mere continuation of a partnership, and, on the facts before it, a new corporation could be found to be the mere continuation of a separately operated, unincorporated line of business (a division run under a fictitious business name) of another corporation that itself continued to exist. The court described successor liability, like alter ego and similar principles, as an equitable doctrine whose issues are examined on their own unique facts, and rejected the argument that successor liability could never attach where the selling entity retained its separate identity and kept operating after the transfer; while there may be circumstances in which successor liability would be inappropriate in that situation, the court held that conclusion does not follow as a matter of law. Under this reading, whether a buyer has become a mere continuation of what it bought depends on all the facts and circumstances rather than on any single element.

THE FOURTH EXCEPTION: A TRANSFER MADE FOR THE FRAUDULENT PURPOSE OF ESCAPING THE SELLER'S DEBTS
The fourth traditional exception stated in Ray v. Alad Corp. is a transfer of assets to the purchaser made for the fraudulent purpose of escaping liability for the seller's debts. In Ray itself there was no indication or contention that the transaction was prompted by any such purpose. Cleveland v. Johnson (2012) illustrates the exception in operation: although the plaintiff there had not expressly proceeded on that theory and the jury was not instructed on it, the jury had found that the individual defendant and the new corporation knowingly acted against the plaintiff's interests by failing to disclose material facts and acted with malice, oppression, or fraud. The Court of Appeal held that substantial evidence supported those findings, from which the necessary conclusion was that the individual had transferred the business's assets to the new corporation and hidden its formation from the plaintiff for the purpose of avoiding liability under the contract with him, so that successor liability would be appropriate on this ground as well as on the mere-continuation ground.

THE PRODUCT-LINE EXCEPTION FOR STRICT PRODUCTS LIABILITY, AND ITS LIMIT TO PRODUCT LIABILITY ACTIONS
Having found that none of the four traditional exceptions applied, the Supreme Court in Ray v. Alad Corp. created a special exception for strict tort liability for defective products. The buyer there had acquired the ladder manufacturer's plant, equipment, inventory, trade name, and goodwill for cash, continued making the same line of ladders under the same name with the same designs and personnel, and solicited the seller's customers with no outward sign of a change in ownership, while the seller dissolved within two months of the sale; the plaintiff was injured by a ladder the seller had made months after that dissolution. The court rested successor liability in those circumstances on three justifications: the virtual destruction of the plaintiff's remedies against the original manufacturer caused by the successor's acquisition of the business; the successor's ability to assume the original manufacturer's risk-spreading role; and the fairness of requiring the successor to assume a responsibility for defective products that was a burden necessarily attached to the goodwill the successor was enjoying. It held that a party which acquires a manufacturing business and continues the output of its line of products under those circumstances assumes strict tort liability for defects in units of the same product line previously manufactured and distributed by the entity from which the business was acquired. Later Court of Appeal decisions have confined the exception to that setting. In Franklin v. USX Corp. (2001), the court summarized Ray's conditions — no viable remedy against the then-nonexistent manufacturer, continued manufacture of the same product line with the same personnel, designs, and customer lists, no outward indication of the change in ownership, and near-identical opportunities to evaluate and pass on production risks — and, following Monarch Bay II and Maloney, declined to expand the product-line exception beyond product liability, concluding that the rule applies only to product liability actions and not to ordinary negligence claims.

THE CONTRAST WITH A STATUTORY MERGER: THE SURVIVING CORPORATION SUCCEEDS TO ALL DEBTS AND LIABILITIES BY OPERATION OF LAW
The successor-liability case law described above concerns a purchase of assets, where the buyer generally does not take on the seller's obligations. A statutory merger under the General Corporation Law works the opposite way by statute. Corporations Code section 1107 provides that, upon a merger, the separate existence of the disappearing corporations ceases and the surviving corporation succeeds, without any other transfer, to all the rights and property of each disappearing corporation and is subject to all of its debts and liabilities in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred them. All rights of creditors and all liens on the property of each constituent corporation are preserved unimpaired, with liens on a disappearing corporation's property limited to the property they affected immediately before the merger took effect. Any action or proceeding pending by or against a disappearing corporation may be prosecuted to judgment, which binds the surviving corporation, or the surviving corporation may be proceeded against or substituted in its place. The de facto merger exception in the case law is the courts' way of treating an asset transaction that has the practical features of a merger as if this statutory succession had occurred.

The California Supreme Court's decision in Ray v. Alad Corp. (1977) opens its legal discussion with the rule ordinarily applied when one corporation purchases the principal assets of another. It held that a party which acquires a manufacturing business and continues the output of its line of products under those circumstances assumes strict tort liability for defects in units of the same product line previously manufactured and distributed by the entity from which the business was acquired. Later Court of Appeal decisions have confined the exception to that setting. In Franklin v. USX Corp. (2001), the court summarized Ray's conditions — no viable remedy against the then-nonexistent manufacturer, continued manufacture of the same product line with the same personnel, designs, and customer lists, no outward indication of the change in ownership, and near-identical opportunities to evaluate and pass on production risks — and, following Monarch Bay II and Maloney, declined to expand the product-line exception beyond product liability, concluding that the rule applies only to product liability actions and not to ordinary negligence claims.

citations.quote: Justification for imposing strict liability upon a successor to a manufacturer under the circumstances here presented rests upon (1) the virtual destruction of the plaintiff’s remedies against the original manufacturer caused by the successor’s acquisition of the business, (2) the successor’s ability to assume the original manufacturer’s risk-spreading role, and (3) the fairness of requiring the successor to assume a responsibility for defective products that was a burden necessarily attached to the original manufacturer’s good will being enjoyed by the successor in the continued operation of the business.

We therefore conclude that a party which acquires a manufacturing business and continues the output of its line of products under the circumstances here presented assumes strict tort liability for defects in units of the same product line previously manufactured and distributed by the entity from which the business was acquired.

It held that imposition of strict liability against the successor to the manufacturer was justified where, as in the case before it, the plaintiff had no viable remedy against the then nonexistent manufacturer of the defective product, the successor to the manufacturer continued to manufacture the same product line as its predecessor, retained the same personnel, used the same designs and customer lists, gave no outward indication of the change in ownership and had opportunities to evaluate production risks and pass on the cost of meeting those risks almost identical to its predecessor’s.
As did those two courts before us, we decline to expand the product line exception beyond the arena of product liability.
Finally, we conclude that the product line successor rule applies only to product liability actions, and is therefore inapplicable to the present case.

(1999) 75 Cal.App.4th 1213 and Maloney v. American Pharmaceutical Co. (1988) 207 Cal.App.3d 282 had already rejected its extension to negligence claims, but neither of those opinions was fetched and their holdings are described here only as Franklin characterizes them. Ray's three justifications were stated as reasons for the result "under the circumstances here presented," and Franklin reads Ray as intending the exception to be limited to those circumstances; whether each of Ray's three justifications is a required element in every case is not stated in the sentences quoted and this sheet does not say so. expectedJSON.body: The successor-liability case law described above concerns a purchase of assets, where the buyer generally does not take on the seller's obligations. A statutory merger under the General Corporation Law works the opposite way by statute. Corporations Code section 1107 provides that, upon a merger, the separate existence of the disappearing corporations ceases and the surviving corporation succeeds, without any other transfer, to all the rights and property of each disappearing corporation and is subject to all of its debts and liabilities in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred them. All rights of creditors and all liens on the property of each constituent corporation are preserved unimpaired, with liens on a disappearing corporation's property limited to the property they affected immediately before the merger took effect. Any action or proceeding pending by or against a disappearing corporation may be prosecuted to judgment, which binds the surviving corporation, or the surviving corporation may be proceeded against or substituted in its place. The de facto merger exception in the case law is the courts' way of treating an asset transaction that has the practical features of a merger as if this statutory succession had occurred.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 1107(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Upon merger pursuant to this chapter the separate existence of the disappearing corporations ceases and the surviving corporation shall succeed, without other transfer, to all the rights and property of each of the disappearing corporations and shall be subject to all the debts and liabilities of each in the same manner as if the surviving corporation had itself incurred them.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 1107(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: All rights of creditors and all liens upon the property of each of the constituent corporations shall be preserved unimpaired, provided that any liens upon property of a disappearing corporation shall be limited to the property affected thereby immediately prior to the time the merger is effective.

citations.case: Cal. Corporations Code § 1107(d) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Any action or proceeding pending by or against any disappearing corporation may be prosecuted to judgment, which shall bind the surviving corporation, or the surviving corporation may be proceeded against or substituted in its place.

expectedJSON.gap: All three quotations are subdivisions of a single section (Corp. Code § 1107) rather than independent sources. The section governs mergers of corporations under Chapter 11 of the General Corporation Law; parallel provisions for limited liability companies and other entities exist elsewhere and are not cited here. The procedure for approving and filing a merger is the subject of this corpus's separate statutory-merger sheet. The final sentence of the body, characterizing the de facto merger exception as the case-law counterpart of this statutory succession, is this sheet's own summary connecting the two clauses and is not a quotation from either source.

expectedJSON.body: Separately from the case law, the Sales and Use Tax Law imposes a statutory successor liability on anyone who buys a business or its stock of goods. Revenue and Taxation Code section 6811 provides that if a person liable for any amount under that law sells out the business or stock of goods, or quits the business, the successors or assigns must withhold enough of the purchase price to cover that amount until the former owner produces a receipt showing it has been paid or a certificate stating that no amount is due. Under section 6812, a purchaser who fails to withhold as required becomes personally liable for the amount required to be withheld, up to the extent of the purchase price valued in money. The agency must, within 60 days after the latest of three dates — its receipt of the purchaser's written request for a certificate, the date of the sale, or the date the former owner's records are made available for audit — either issue the certificate or mail the purchaser notice of the amount that must be paid as a condition of issuing it; failure to mail that notice releases the purchaser from any further obligation to withhold, and the successor's obligation cannot be enforced later than three years after the agency is notified of the purchase. Section 6814 provides that the obligation is enforced by serving a notice of successor liability, that the successor may petition for reconsideration, and that a successor whose failure to withhold was due to reasonable cause and circumstances beyond its control, despite ordinary care and without willful neglect, may be relieved of any penalty included in the notice.

citations.quote: If the purchaser of a business or stock of goods fails to withhold from the purchase price as required, he or she becomes personally liable for the payment of the amount required to be withheld by him or her to the extent of the purchase price, valued in money.

(2) For purposes of paragraph (1), the latest of the following dates shall apply: (A) The date the board receives a written request from the purchaser for a certificate. (B) The date of the sale of the business or stock of goods. (C) The date the former owner’s records are made available for audit.

citations.case: Cal. Revenue and Taxation Code § 6812(c) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: Failure of the board to mail the notice referred to in subdivision (b) will release the purchaser from any further obligation to withhold from the purchase price as above provided. The last date upon which the obligation of the successor may be enforced shall be not later than three years after the date the board is notified of the purchase of the business or stock of goods.

citations.quote: The obligation of the successor shall be enforced by serving a notice of successor liability on the person. The notice shall be served in the manner prescribed for service of a notice of a deficiency determination, not later than three years after the date the board is notified of the purchase of the business or stock of goods. The successor may petition for reconsideration in the manner provided in Article 5 (commencing with Section 6561) of Chapter 5 of this part.

citations.quote: If the board finds that a successor’s failure to withhold a sufficient amount of the purchase price to cover the amount owed by the former owner is due to reasonable cause and circumstances beyond the successor’s control, and occurred notwithstanding the exercise of ordinary care and in the absence of willful neglect, the successor may be relieved of any penalty included in the notice of successor liability.

expectedJSON.gap: All quotations are from Article 7 of Chapter 6 of the Sales and Use Tax Law (Rev. & Tax. Code §§ 6811–6815), a single statutory article, rather than independent sources. The sections' text refers to "the board," the term used when the State Board of Equalization administered this law; responsibility for administering sales and use taxes was transferred to the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration by later legislation that this sheet does not quote, and the clause body uses "the agency" for that reason while the quotations reproduce the statutory wording. The sheet does not describe the form of request for a certificate, the audit process, or the amounts of any penalty, and does not address the parallel successor provisions for other state taxes and fees. Section 6813, which addresses when the certificate may be issued after payment or security, is not quoted.

expectedJSON.body: The Unemployment Insurance Code contains a parallel successor regime for an employer's unpaid contributions. Under section 1731, any person or employing unit that acquires the organization, trade, or business of an employer, or substantially all of its assets, must withhold in trust money or other property sufficient to cover any contributions, interest, and penalties due or unpaid from that employer until the employer produces a certificate from the department stating that none are due; if the employer does not produce the certificate, the acquirer must pay the amount or value withheld to the department at the time of the acquisition. Section 1732 provides that, on request of either party to the acquisition, the department must within 30 days issue either a certificate or a statement of the amount claimed to be due, and that its failure to do so within 30 days is deemed equivalent to a certificate that nothing is due. If a statement issues, the stated amount is withheld and paid to the department, but not more than the purchase price. The issuance of a certificate, or the failure to issue either document within 30 days, does not release the selling employer from liability for contributions later determined to be due, but does release the acquiring person or employing unit from any further liability for them.

citations.quote: Any person or employing unit that acquires the organization, trade or business, or substantially all the assets thereof, of an employer shall withhold in trust money or other property sufficient in amount or value to cover the amount of any contributions, interest and penalties due or unpaid from such employer until such employer produces a certificate from the department stating that no contributions, interest or penalties are due. If such employer does not produce such certificate, the acquiring person or employing unit shall pay the amount or the value of the property so withheld to the department at the time of such acquisition.

citations.quote: Upon request of either of the parties to an acquisition as described in Section 1731, the department shall within 30 days issue a certificate, or a statement showing the amount of any contributions, interest and penalties claimed to be due. The failure to issue a certificate or a statement within the period of 30 days shall be deemed equivalent to the issuance of a certificate stating that no contributions, interest or penalties are due.

citations.quote: If the department issues a statement showing the amount of contributions, interest and penalties claimed to be due, the amount stated therein shall be withheld and paid to the department such amount, however, not to exceed the purchase price. The issuance of any certificate stating that no contributions, interest and penalties are due, or the failure to issue such certificate or statement within the period of 30 days shall not release the employer from liability on account of any contributions, interest and penalties then or thereafter determined to be due from him, but shall release the acquiring person or employing unit from any further liability on account of any such contributions, interest and penalties.

expectedJSON.gap: Both quotations are from Article 2 of Chapter 7 of Part 1 of the Unemployment Insurance Code (§§ 1731–1736), a single statutory article, rather than independent sources; the remaining sections of that article, which address officers and fiduciaries, are not quoted. "The department" in these sections is the Employment Development Department, as defined elsewhere in the code in a section not fetched for this sheet. The statute does not specify a form of request or the mechanics of the withholding "in trust," and this sheet supplies none. Whether the acquirer also succeeds to the seller's unemployment insurance experience rating (a separate question governed by other sections of the code) is not addressed.

expectedJSON.body: Since January 1, 2021, the Labor Code has contained its own successorship rule for wage judgments. Under section 200.3, a successor to a judgment debtor is liable for any wages, damages, and penalties owed to any of the judgment debtor's former workforce under a final judgment, once the time to appeal has expired and no appeal is pending. Successorship is established by meeting any one of four criteria: (1) using substantially the same facilities or substantially the same workforce to offer substantially the same services as the judgment debtor (a factor that does not apply to employers who keep the same workforce under the Labor Code's displaced-worker retention provisions); (2) having substantially the same owners or managers that control labor relations as the judgment debtor; (3) employing as a managing agent any person who directly controlled the wages, hours, or working conditions of the judgment debtor's affected workforce; or (4) operating a business in the same industry where an owner, partner, officer, or director is an immediate family member of any owner, partner, officer, or director of the judgment debtor. The section states that it does not limit other means of establishing successor liability for wages, damages, and penalties — so the case-law grounds described in the earlier clauses remain available alongside it.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 200.3(a) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: (a) A successor to a judgment debtor shall be liable for any wages, damages, and penalties owed to any of the judgment debtor’s former workforce pursuant to a final judgment, after the time to appeal therefrom has expired and for which no appeal therefrom is pending. Successorship is established upon meeting any of the following criteria: (1) Uses substantially the same facilities or substantially the same workforce to offer substantially the same services as the judgment debtor. This factor does not apply to employers who maintain the same workforce pursuant to Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 1060) of Part 3. (2) Has substantially the same owners or managers that control the labor relations as the judgment debtor. (3) Employs as a managing agent any person who directly controlled the wages, hours, or working conditions of the affected workforce of the judgment debtor. The term managing agent has the same meaning as in subdivision (b) of Section 3294 of the Civil Code. (4) Operates a business in the same industry and the business has an owner, partner, officer, or director who is an immediate family member of any owner, partner, officer, or director of the judgment debtor.

citations.case: Cal. Labor Code § 200.3(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.quote: This section shall not be construed to limit other means of establishing successor liability for wages, damages, and penalties.

expectedJSON.gap: Both quotations are subdivisions of a single statutory section (Lab. Code § 200.3, added by Stats. 2020, ch. 357 (AB 3075), effective January 1, 2021) rather than independent sources. The section applies only to amounts owed under a final judgment for wages, damages, and penalties; it does not itself create successor liability for wage claims that have not been reduced to judgment. The cross-reference in criterion (1) is to Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 1060) of Part 3 of Division 2 of the Labor Code (the Displaced Janitor Opportunity Act), and "managing agent" in criterion (3) takes its meaning from Civil Code section 3294(b); neither of those provisions was fetched for this sheet. No published appellate decision construing § 200.3 was located through the sources consulted, and none is cited.
